scope.notes: Inventory in progress (261 rows). Covers Exalted: The Fair Folk's Chapter Three character-creation overview (separately for noble and common raksha, since the two follow different Attribute/Background baselines), the four base castes (Diplomat/Entertainer/Warrior/Worker) with their Caste Abilities/Grace/Controlling Grace/Associations/Sobriquets, the twelve named noble hybrid castes (ascendant/shadowed caste pairings), the five Graces (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword/Heart) with full dot tables plus their general forging rules, the Bedlam mechanic (this splat's Limit-Trait analog) including all four Virtue-specific Curses and their Lures, the five new Fair Folk Backgrounds (Birth, Freehold, Gossamer, Retinue, Style), the altered Backgrounds (Artifact, Familiar, Manse, Backing/Contacts/Influence) and the excluded ones (Followers, Resources), a set of core signature mechanics (innate Wyld-damage immunity, Craft (Glamour), Wyld stunts/bonuses, Gossamer-and-Glamour Charm fuel, Mutation, Shaping Actions/Reality Shaping, Shaping Combat basics, Oaths, Cold-Wrought Iron), all five of Chapter Five's per-Grace Charm trees in full (Heart/Nirguna 14 rows, Staff/Nirvikalpa 12 rows, Cup/Dharma 48 rows, Ring/Nirvishesha 78 rows, Sword/Nishkriya 42 rows -- pp. 155-205/PDF 156-206 combined), and now the universal, non-Grace-gated Assumption-type Charm tree in full (shinma Nirakara, 'the Mask'; 21 Charm rows, pp. 149-155/PDF 150-156), the Charms every raksha uses to take shape and exist within Creation at all, with no minimum Grace requirement of their own: two independent gateway roots (Assumption of Elemental Shape, consolidated across its five Air/Earth/Fire/Water/Wood variants like Bastion of the Self, and Assumption of Cerements and Bone for the Underworld) feeding a line of region-tainting Charms (Assumption of the Person's/Land's/City's Heart, Living Kingdom, Wyld-Tainted Land) and the permanent Mad God Mien (which resolves a forward reference from the Ring Grace tree's Extinction of Desire), plus two further sub-trees: Elemental Influence (Sovereign Elemental Shape, Element-Weaving Style, Elemental Invocation; World-Angering Elemental Mastery, Teeth of the World; Elemental Transformation and Mercurial Shape) and Emotional Influence, explicitly framed in the book as a worked example of a personalized non-elemental Assumption-type Charm tree (Assumption of Dreams and Passion, Elegant Muse Attitude, Emotion-Weaving Style, Emotional Invocation, Unwanted Obsession Provocation Technique, Essence-Disrobing Passion). One naming slip was flagged: Assumption of the Wyld-Tainted Land's own text says it 'functions as Assumption of the Kingdom's Heart,' a Charm name that does not exist anywhere in the book; its stated Prerequisite Charms line and tree diagram both confirm it actually branches off Assumption of the City's Heart. A seventh pass then added the 'Vexing' rules and 'Questing' sidebar (2 rows, pp. 147-148/PDF 148-149, Sword-shaping-combat-adjacent material immediately preceding the Assumption-type Charm tree): the general Vexing mechanic (seizing possessions/waypoints/behemoth-essence from a loser of a Sword-shaping contest, plus the Willpower + Essence resistance roll for Creation-born victims without a Sword Grace) and the Questing sidebar (raksha who deliberately provoke unshaped god-monsters into shaping contests to win artifacts/spells/servants). An eighth pass then completed all of Chapter Five's remaining material (26 rows, pp. 205-211/PDF 206-212): Glamour Sorcery (the raksha's Artifact-Background-purchased spell system -- five Circle tiers, Waking/Dreaming/Desire/Samadhi/Shinma, plus its framework and countermagic sidebar), Wyld Artifacts (the Ring-forged-treasure category plus three named examples -- Resonant Chorus Bow, Hundred Color Shaping Lens, Artifact Waypoint), Adjurations (the world-shaping-oath category plus its 'How Inconvenient' framing sidebar and five named oath tiers -- Samhara/Sthiti/Anugraha/Tirobhava/Srishti, aspected respectively to Sword/Ring/Cup/Staff/Heart), Behemoths (the Sword-aspected monstrous-companion-artifact category plus Behemoth Powers, three named tiers -- Fey Beast, Daikaiju, Deep Wyld Horror -- and the unique, gm-only legendary example Ishiika, once tamed by the lost Prince Balor), and the apparent sixth shinma Nirupadhika, the Way (determined to be real, rules-complete, narrowly-scoped player-facing content -- two Charms, Forging the Way Grace and Perfect Reckoning Technique -- rather than either a standard sixth Grace or pure GM lore; see rulesNotes for the full determination). This pass also corrected a one-page offset in this file's own prior page estimates for Behemoths and Nirupadhika, found via direct visual confirmation against the rendered page images (see rulesNotes). With this pass, Chapter Five: Raksha Magic is now fully inventoried end to end (261 rows total). A subsequent triage pass then reviewed Chapters One, Two, Six and Seven in full (263 rows total): Merits/Flaws specific to Fair Folk are now definitively confirmed absent from the entire book (see rulesNotes for the full search), and exactly two more genuinely player-facing rows were found and added -- the Gossamer Manta (a purchasable Artifact-Background vehicle from Chapter One's Rakshastan geography material) and Fair Folk Experience and Training Time (Chapter Seven's post-creation advancement-cost table). Chapter Two's lore and Chapter Six's Mountain Folk (a wholly separate playable-adjacent race with its own extensive character creation) were confirmed to contain no further Fair Folk-specific player-facing mechanics; see rulesNotes for the complete triage writeup. A tenth pass then closed the universal Merits/Flaws gap this book itself confirmed absent (see the ninth pass's book-wide text search above): 73 of the 88 rows in the Exalted Players Guide's Chapter One, 'Merits and Flaws' (pp. 18-41/PDF 19-42), were derived for Fair Folk (37 merits + 36 flaws) from Lunar's already-verified transcription of that universal chapter, rather than an independent re-read, since each Lunar row's own notes already capture splat-specific eligibility/cost caveats verbatim and the chapter is explicitly universal across all five planned families (336 rows total). 15 of the 88 were skipped as inapplicable (7 merits: Terrestrial Bloodline, Past Lives, Sworn Brotherhood, Taint's Warning, Legendary Breeding, Eternal Vow, Brigid's Heir; 8 flaws: Limited Forms, Known Anathema, Chimera, Permanent Caste Mark, Greater Curse, Beacon of Power, Death-Taint, Throwback) -- either explicitly restricted to other splats by the source's own header text, or ruled out by the raksha's own nature as beings of pure Wyld/chaos that are not Exalted at all (no Essence-reincarnation cycle to key Past Lives/Throwback off of, no anima or Caste Mark for Permanent Caste Mark/Beacon of Power to merge, no access to core Exalted Sorcery for Brigid's Heir, and no blood-lineage/breeding concept for Terrestrial Bloodline/Legendary Breeding). Several included rows required reinterpretation for the raksha's own framework rather than Creation-born Exalted assumptions: Large Size/Small reframed around a raksha's Assumption-type shapeshifting Charms instead of Lunar forms; Cache/Debt reframed around the Gossamer Background instead of Resources (which raksha exclude entirely), using Gossamer's own documented 'effective Resources' dot table as the bridging mechanic; Vice/Callous cross-referenced to Bedlam (this splat's Limit-Trait analog) instead of the Great Curse; Unskilled's Favored-Ability floor reframed as a Caste-Ability floor; Prodigy included by analogy to Dragon-Blooded/Sidereal (whose Caste/Favored Ability structure a raksha's own closely resembles) rather than excluded by the silence of the source text; and Destiny/Dark Fate/Unbidden Oracle included as selectable despite a flagged conceptual tension, since raksha are canonically native to the Wyld outside Creation's Loom of Fate that those three Traits represent. Mutation and Weak Essence were flagged as unusually strong fits rather than adaptations, since raksha are literally Wyld-stuff given shape and every raksha starts with Essence 2 exactly as Weak Essence's own 'other magical beings' clause requires. Every judgment call is flagged verbatim in the affected row's own notes field. An eleventh pass then added two small sets of universal (non-splat-restricted) artifact catalog rows, bringing the total to 351: 6 rows (artifact-ghost-cestus, artifact-sling-bow-of-ice, artifact-the-golden-viper, artifact-land-ship, artifact-singing-staff, artifact-eye-of-autochthon) derived from Lunar's already-verified transcription of the Exalted Storyteller's Companion's universal 'Further Wonders' artifact catalog (Chapter Four, printed pp. 77-80/PDF 78-81) -- a fifth source book added to this family's manifest -- re-cited to the same pages with no independent re-read, since none of the 6 rows carries splat-restricting text that would exclude Fair Folk (raksha have their own Essence rating and mote pool identical to the Exalted, per fair-folk-creation-overview-common / -noble, so the several 'Essence-manipulating wielder' requirements transfer without reinterpretation); and 9 rows freshly transcribed from a sixth source book, Savage Seas, whose 'Artifacts of the Waves' section (Chapter Four, printed pp. 123-127/PDF 124-128) is likewise a universal naval-artifact catalog, unlike that chapter's earlier Solar/Dragon-Blooded-only 'Magics of the Sea' Charms section (printed pp. 114-122), which remains correctly out of scope. Those 9 rows -- Cargo Preservation Spindles, Armor of Aquatic Puissance, Steelsilk Sails, Storm Sapphire, Cord of Winds, Wavecleaver Daiklaive, Light Implosion Bow, Lightning Ballista, and a reference-only Artifact Ship Weapons summary table -- are all disposition selectable except the summary table (reference-only). The Light Implosion Bow is the strongest fit in the whole batch: its own text explicitly names 'any Exalted type and also Fair Folk and possibly others' as capable of channeling Essence into it, the only artifact in this pass to name raksha by name rather than requiring inference. The Lightning Ballista is flagged as a judgment call: the source calls it 'powerless in the hands of the unExalted,' but its actual mechanical requirement is only that 'the firer must be able to manipulate Essence,' which a raksha satisfies; see that row's own notes for the full reasoning. Two low-zoom transcription errors (the Storm Sapphire Effect Table's Black Sapphire column, and the Lightning Ballista's hearthstone-variant Artifact rating) were caught and corrected via high-zoom re-renders of the affected table regions before this pass was considered complete; see those rows' own notes. See rulesNotes for the full accounting of this pass, including the Fair-Folk-specific 'Mote' (physical shell) vs. 'motes' (Essence currency) terminology check performed for every row. A final cross-splat supplement-triage pass added 14 rows from Exalted: Blood and Salt, a regional sourcebook about An-Teng and the Lintha Family. A full cover-to-cover read confirmed the vast majority of the book's Background/Artifact/Charm/Sorcery/Hearthstone keyword hits sit inside NPC/monster stat blocks (GM-only reference material), but a smaller set of genuinely player-facing content was found and transcribed: a 'Character Backgrounds' sidebar (printed p. 63/PDF 65) reinterpreting what dot ratings in the Allies, Backing, and Contacts Backgrounds mean for a character with Lintha Family ties; a 'Navigating the Approaches' sidebar on the same page giving the Sail-based difficulty check for reaching the hidden floating city of Bluehaven; four regional 'Character Concepts' lists (Shore Lands, Middle Lands, High Lands, Bluehaven; printed pp. 27/32/36/63, PDF 29/34/38/65); seven new Artifacts from Chapter Three's 'Wonders of the Southwest' (Automaton Assassin, Sailcutter Chakram, Ancestor Sash, the Seven Lotus Crown, the Masks That Command the Animals, the Coral Crown, and the Talisman of the Cult of Dukantha, which grants Infernal sorcery access independent of the bearer's own normal sorcery Charms); one new Hearthstone (the Jewel of Stability, Earth Manse •••); three mundane equipment items (Fire Arrow, Southern Fire Arrow, Water Shoes). None of this content is splat-restricted, so -- following this project's established precedent for universal cross-splat content -- it was transcribed once (into Lunar's inventory as the master copy) and copied into all five families' inventories in the same pass, with only each row's `compatibility` text adjusted per family. Four artifacts (Cord of Winds, Light Implosion Bow, Steelsilk Sails, Storm Sapphire) that this family's inventory had already transcribed from Savage Seas are reprinted verbatim in Blood and Salt ('repeated here for ease of reference,' per the book's own text); rather than duplicate rows, a REPRINT NOTE was appended to each existing row's `notes` field. The Seven Lotus Crown and Coral Crown are both marked selectable but flagged as narrowly restricted to a specific narrative title-holder (the rightful High Queen of An-Teng and the true King of the Vodonik, respectively) rather than freely purchasable at character creation. The remainder of the book (all NPC/monster/antagonist stat-block content, including the many 'Suggested Charms' and 'Backgrounds: ...' NPC listings) was reviewed and confirmed out of scope.

Universal Merits & Flaws chapter (Chapter One); most entries apply to any character type and were derived for Fair Folk (raksha) from Lunar's already-verified transcription, re-citing and reinterpreting them for a splat that is not Exalted

Naval/nautical sourcebook; Chapter Four's Artifacts of the Waves section (splat-unrestricted physical naval artifacts) transcribed directly from the source PDF for Fair Folk

Its genuinely player-facing content -- a Lintha-connection Backgrounds reinterpretation sidebar, an approach-to-Bluehaven navigation rule, four regional character-concept lists, seven new Artifacts, one new Hearthstone, three mundane equipment items, and (for splats with standard sorcery access) two new Terrestrial Circle spells -- was transcribed into this family's inventory; four reprinted artifacts and (where applicable) a reprinted Hearthstone and two reprinted/superseded spells received citation notes on their existing rows instead of new duplicate rows.

rulesNotes: This PDF has a real, selectable text layer (confirmed via direct PyMuPDF text extraction on multiple sample pages); it is not image-only like the Lunar/Abyssal source PDFs. Text was extracted directly and cross-checked by visually rendering and reading a sample of pages (character-creation summary tables, Grace dot tables, Background dot tables, the Noble Castes pages, and the Storyteller-only 'unshaped' Charm-suggestion sidebar) with the same render-pdf-pages.py + Read-tool workflow used for image-based books, since dot-rating tables and sidebar boxes are exactly the layout that can scramble during plain text extraction. No scrambling was found in the sampled pages; the extracted text order matched the visual layout in every spot-checked case.

Printed page numbers in this book run exactly 1 less than the PDF (physical) page number for the copy used to build this inventory (PDF page = printed page + 1); both are recorded on every citation. This was confirmed both from the Table of Contents (printed page 7, PDF page 8) and from directly reading the printed folio number embedded in the extracted text of dozens of sampled pages.

Fair Folk (raksha) are structurally unlike Solar/Abyssal/Dragon-Blooded/Lunar creation: there are no Attributes-and-Abilities-only Charms, no five Castes shared uniformly by common and noble characters, and no single universal Limit-Trait analog. Common raksha have one feeding Virtue/Grace/caste; noble raksha have two (an 'ascendant' and a 'shadowed' caste), and the ascendant/shadowed pairing across the four base castes produces twelve distinct named noble-caste archetypes (Anarch, Luminary, Panjandrum, Artisan, Courtier, Xia, Eshu, Imperial Raksha, Strategos, Scribe, Ornamental Raksha, Cataphract). Charms are keyed to five Grace Traits (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword/Heart) rather than to Attributes or Abilities. The Limit-Trait role is filled by Bedlam, which is Virtue-specific rather than universal: each of the four Virtues has its own named Curse (Hubris/Compassion, Namelessness/Conviction, Alienation/Temperance, Meekness-or-Terror/Valor) with its own trigger and recovery condition, plus a mandatory Lure once any Virtue reaches 3+.

'Heart's Blood' does not appear anywhere in this book as Fair Folk terminology; the raksha's core existential Trait is instead the Heart Grace (fixed rating, not freely purchasable), and their wealth/Charm-fuel resource is called Gossamer, not Heart's Blood. No conflation with the Lunar Exalted's unrelated use of similar terms was found or assumed.

Common raksha and noble raksha are covered as two separate character-creation-overview rows in this inventory (fair-folk-creation-overview-common and fair-folk-creation-overview-noble) rather than one combined row, because the book presents them as two materially different baselines (0-dot vs. 3-dot starting Attributes, 0 vs. 10 free Background dots, 1 vs. 3 Favored Abilities, a cheaper Specialty cost for commoners, a cheaper Major Grace cost for nobles) with two separate condensed summary boxes, not one shared creation track with minor caste variation.

Chapter Five's Charm material (pp. 129-213/PDF 130-214, immediately before Chapter Six: The Mountain Folk starts at printed p. 213/PDF 214) is far larger than a single pass can cover: after the general-rules content already inventoried (gossamer/glamour, mutation, shaping actions, shaping combat basics, oaths, cold-wrought iron), it contains a universal, non-Grace-gated Assumption-type Charm tree (the gateway shinma Nirakara, 'the Mask') plus five per-Grace Charm trees, each opened by prose describing its shinma and closed or interleaved with combat-mechanics sections (shaping attack/soak/wound-penalty rules for that Grace) that were already summarized at the mechanical-overview level in shaping-combat-basics. Across three passes, this inventory has now fully covered three of the five: the Heart Grace tree (shinma Nirguna, pp. 155-159/PDF 156-160 -- Name Charms, Bedlam-Influencing Charms [notable for drawing branches from all five Graces rather than just Heart], Dodge Charms, Resistance Charms), the Staff Grace tree (shinma Nirvikalpa, pp. 193-196/PDF 194-197 -- the 10-Charm 'Laughing Monster Style' combat tree plus the separate 2-Charm 'Society-Forging Charms' tree, Oath Gossamer and Eight-Corner Ring Binding), and the Cup Grace tree (shinma Dharma, pp. 159-171/PDF 160-172 -- 48 Charms across Cup Combat Charms [including the named 'Spirit-Twisting Obsession Style' sub-tree], Feeding Charms, Addiction Charms, World-Shaping Charms and Virtue-Shaping Charms). The Cup tree and this pass's continuation into the Ring tree both surfaced several Charms that are explicitly gated on a different Grace than the section they sit in (e.g. Beguilement and Spite-Summoning Malediction, Cup-tree Charms explicitly marked 'Minimum Staff' and 'This is a Staff-shaping Charm'; Undetectable Lie, a Ring Combat Charm with the same pattern) -- the same cross-Grace-crossover pattern already flagged for the Heart tree's Bedlam-Influencing Charms, now confirmed as a recurring structural feature of this Charm material rather than a one-off. This pass completed the Ring Grace tree's first three named sub-sections (shinma Nirvishesha, pp. 171-192/PDF 172-193 -- by far the largest of the five): Ring Combat Charms (16 Charms, pp. 171-175/PDF 172-176, with two independent roots converging at Sorrowful Firmament Resonance), All-Consuming God-Monster Style (6 Charms, pp. 175-178/PDF 176-179, a Stance-type transformation tree granting a purchasable 'God-Monster Body' with a paraphrased sample gift menu, culminating in the self-annihilating capstone Chimera Exultation), Body-Strengthening Charms (5 Charms, pp. 178-180/PDF 179-181, a stacking natural-soak progression plus the standalone Ox-Body Technique) and Creation-Based Crafting (3 Charms, pp. 180-181/PDF 181-182). The large Glamour Charms section (pp. 181-192/PDF 182-193), including the 'Forging the (Grace) Grace' Charms that let raksha grant Grace Traits to Creation-born characters and the Freehold-anchoring Forging the Stronghold/Glory/Fountainhead/Throne Room Charms, and the Sword tree (Nishkriya, pp. 196-203/PDF 197-204) remain for future passes, in that page order.

A short, apparently sixth Grace called 'the Way' (shinma Nirupadhika) surfaces on p. 212 (PDF 213), immediately before Chapter Six begins, with a 'Forging the Way Grace' Charm and a 'Perfect Reckoning Technique' Charm. It postdates and sits outside the five Graces (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword/Heart) established in Chapter Four's Traits chapter and used throughout this inventory's character-creation and Grace rows; it has not been inventoried or cross-referenced against the existing five-Grace model and needs dedicated review (likely alongside Glamour Sorcery, Wyld Artifacts, Adjurations and Behemoths, which immediately precede it on pp. 205-212/PDF 206-213) before any claims are made about whether it is a real player-facing sixth Grace, an artifact/enchantment category, or setting-specific NPC material.

A fourth pass added the Ring Grace tree's first Glamour Charms tree (14 Charms, pp. 181-185/PDF 182-186), which crafts/summons servants, territory and wealth for a raksha's court. Monstrous Conceit continues the cross-Grace-crossover pattern already noted above: it is gated on both the existing Undetectable Lie (Ring Combat) and the new Glamour Charm, despite sitting in the Glamour Charms section. The 'Greater Arts of Glamour' sub-section (pp. 185-192/PDF 186-193) -- the Forging the (Grace) Grace Charms and Freehold-anchoring Forging the Stronghold/Glory/Fountainhead/Throne Room Charms -- remains for the next pass.

A fifth pass added the Ring Grace tree's 'Greater Arts of Glamour' sub-section (18 Charms, pp. 185-192/PDF 186-193), which finishes the entire Ring Grace tree. Forging the Heart Grace (off Shape-Forged Servant) branches to the four 'Forging the (Grace) Grace' Charms (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword) and to Forging the Arcane Redoubt (which anchors a Freehold's eternal bonefire and branches to the four parallel Forging the Stronghold/Glory/Fountainhead/Throne Room Charms). All four Grace-granting Charms together feed Gaping Virtue Mouth (-> Iron Nightmare Muzzle, Ecstatic Reproduction Style, and the Staff-shaping crossover Akshata Sexual Methodology). Forging the Heart Grace also feeds the consolidated Great Works of the (Grace) row (four variants packed into one row, matching Bastion of the Self's precedent) -> the consolidated Unshaped (Grace) Transformation row -> the Sword-crossover Behemoth-Forging Meditation and the self-annihilating capstone Extinction of Desire. The same pass then began the fifth and final per-Grace tree, Sword (Nishkriya, the Sword), completing its Sword Combat Charms section in full (27 Charms, pp. 196-202/PDF 197-203): two independent roots (God-Humbling Victory Sword, Host-Summoning Glory of Command) plus a third root (Scattering the Foe) feeding two further lines that converge on capstones Defining the Parameters of Battle and Fearsome Mien, and the named sub-style 'World-Devouring Warlord Style' (9 Charms) culminating in Preemptive Declaration of Victory. One diagram/header naming mismatch was flagged (Waypoint-Sealing Technique, labeled 'Waypoint Sealing Stance' in its tree diagram despite being Type: Reflexive, not Stance-type). Only the Sword Grace tree's separate 'Mutation Charms' section (pp. 202-205/PDF 203-206) remains to finish all five per-Grace Charm trees; it is next for a future pass.

The same fifth pass then completed the Sword Grace tree's 'Mutation Charms' section (15 Charms, pp. 202-205/PDF 203-206) -- a set of individually purchasable Charms of Shape rather than a branching combat tree, nearly all with no Charm prerequisite, save the linear Hundred-Hand Style -> Millipede Mind -> Grace of the Infinite Revolving Spheres / Harmonious Primordial Spirit line (which explicitly stacks with its own prerequisites rather than replacing them). Racing Dragon Speed is flagged as an outlier: unlike every other repurchasable Charm in this Sword-Grace section, its repurchase cap is keyed to the raksha's Compassion rather than her Sword or Valor; this was double-checked against the rendered page image. With this section's completion, **all five of Chapter Five's per-Grace Charm trees (Heart, Staff, Cup, Ring, Sword) are now fully inventoried** (212 rows total). The next largest remaining block of Chapter Five is the universal, non-Grace-gated Assumption-type Charm tree (Nirakara, 'the Mask'; pp. 148-155/PDF 149-156), which several already-inventoried rows reference by name but which has not itself been reviewed.

A sixth pass completed the universal, non-Grace-gated Assumption-type Charm tree in full (shinma Nirakara, 'the Mask'; 21 Charms, pp. 149-155/PDF 150-156) -- the Charms every raksha uses to become a shaped creature capable of existing within Creation, none of which carry a minimum Grace requirement of their own (a raksha's Combo experience cost for one is instead twice its Minimum Essence). Two independent gateway roots were found: Assumption of Elemental Shape (consolidated into one row across its five Air/Earth/Fire/Water/Wood variants, matching the Bastion of the Self precedent) and, for the Underworld specifically, Assumption of Cerements and Bone. From the elemental root, a line of region-tainting Charms runs Assumption of the Person's Heart -> Assumption of the Land's Heart -> Assumption of the City's Heart -> Assumption of a Living Kingdom / Assumption of the Wyld-Tainted Land, capped by the permanent, no-prerequisite Mad God Mien -- this last Charm resolves a forward reference left open by the Ring Grace tree's self-annihilating capstone Extinction of Desire. Two further named sub-trees round out the section: Elemental Influence (Sovereign Elemental Shape -> Element-Weaving Style -> Elemental Invocation, with Sovereign Elemental Shape separately feeding World-Angering Elemental Mastery -> Teeth of the World, and Elemental Transformation -> Mercurial Shape) and Emotional Influence, which the book explicitly presents as a worked example of building a personalized non-elemental Assumption-type Charm tree (Assumption of Dreams and Passion -> Elegant Muse Attitude -> Emotion-Weaving Style -> Emotional Invocation -> Unwanted Obsession Provocation Technique -> Essence-Disrobing Passion). One naming slip was flagged and double-checked against the rendered page image: Assumption of the Wyld-Tainted Land's own text claims to function 'as Assumption of the Kingdom's Heart,' a Charm name that does not exist anywhere in the book; both its stated Prerequisite Charms line and the tree diagram confirm it actually branches off Assumption of the City's Heart, so the reference is treated as a naming slip rather than corrected or reinterpreted. With this tree's completion (233 rows total), the largest remaining blocks of Chapter Five are the short 'Vexing' rules and 'Questing' sidebar (pp. 147-148/PDF 148-149, immediately preceding this tree, not yet inventoried) and Glamour Sorcery / Wyld Artifacts / Adjurations / Behemoths (pp. 205-212/PDF 206-213).

A seventh pass added the 'Vexing' rules and 'Questing' sidebar (2 rows, pp. 147-148/PDF 148-149): Effects of Damage (Sword damage marked against Valor + Sword, loser is vexed once that sum is exceeded), Vexing (seizing possessions/waypoints/Graces up to the loser's Sword Grace, capped at 5 total artifact levels seized, with a raksha's own Heart Grace sacrosanct unless her Sword Grace is broken), Vexing Places (claiming a waypoint via a 3-mote commitment), Vexing the Unshaped (ripping a fresh three-dot behemoth from an unshaped's Sword Grace, or improving an existing one, at most once per story per unshaped), and Vexing Creatures of Creation (a Willpower + Essence resistance roll for Creation-born victims with no Sword Grace, with Exaltation-tier bonus dice) -- all folded into one vexing-mechanic row, plus a separate questing-sidebar row for the boxed Questing rules. The Sword Grace's shaping-weapon stat table (Entanglement, Extras, Hazard, Horror, Monster, Mutant Warleader, Nishkriya Mask, Personal Prowess) on the same page was deliberately not inventoried as its own row, per the same individual-shaping-weapon exclusion already applied to shaping-combat-basics. Resume point for the next pass: Glamour Sorcery / Wyld Artifacts / Adjurations / Behemoths (pp. 205-212/PDF 206-213), then the apparent sixth 'Way' Grace (Nirupadhika, p. 212/PDF 213).

An eighth pass added Glamour Sorcery in full (7 rows, pp. 205-207/PDF 206-208): the framework row (glamour-sorcery-overview, folding in the short 'Spell Abilities' lorekeeper-mechanic subsection) and the 'Glamour Sorcery and Countermagic' sidebar (glamour-sorcery-countermagic), plus the five named Circle tiers as purchasable Artifact-Background options -- Waking Circle Spell (Artifact •), Dreaming Circle Spell (Artifact ••), Desire Circle Spell (Artifact •••), Samadhi Circle Spell (Artifact ••••, restricted to a raksha who owns his own Heart Grace), and Shinma Circle Spell (Artifact •••••). Each tier is built from its own mutation-point budget (10 to 18 points) requiring at least one Assumption-type Charm mutation, with its own invocation cost in motes/gossamer/scenes and its own Cup-shaping-weapon stat defaults; higher tiers (Desire, Samadhi, Shinma) additionally overcome characters who would otherwise be immune to a work of glamour, forcing them to use a stunt or Charm to see through it instead. This resolves a forward reference: the already-inventoried artifact-background-fair-folk row names glamour spells, behemoths, adjurations, and 'the tools of the Ring' as the treasures raksha actually buy with Artifact Background dots, and this pass supplies the mechanical framework and named examples for the first of those four categories.

The same eighth pass added Wyld Artifacts in full (4 rows, pp. 207-208/PDF 208-209): the framework row (wyld-artifacts-overview -- the Ring-shaping self-crafting bonus, and why only a few Wyld artifacts double as Ring-shaping weapons) plus three named examples as purchasable Artifact-Background options -- Resonant Chorus Bow (Artifact •), Hundred Color Shaping Lens (Artifact ••), and Artifact Waypoint (Artifact •••+, an enchanted mobile Ring-shaping weapon built from one or more waypoints).

The same eighth pass added Adjurations in full (7 rows, pp. 208-210/PDF 209-211): the framework row (adjurations-overview -- unbreakable-oath mechanics, the catastrophic-botch consequence of involuntarily breaking one, and the Freehold-wide Throne-Room-sworn-adjuration rule), the 'How Inconvenient Are a Raksha's Oaths?' framing sidebar (adjurations-how-inconvenient-sidebar, disposition reference-only since it sets tone/design intent rather than adding a mechanic), and the five named oath tiers as purchasable Artifact-Background options, each aspected to one of the five core Graces -- Samhara Oath (Artifact •, Sword), Sthiti Oath (Artifact ••, Ring), Anugraha Oath (Artifact •••, Cup), Tirobhava Oath (Artifact ••••, Staff), and Srishti Oath (Artifact •••••, Heart), each with its own mutation-point budget (2 to 6 points, with the Anugraha/Cup and Tirobhava/Staff tiers halving the mutation cost for the swearing raksha, rounding up) and shaping-weapon stat defaults.

The same eighth pass added Behemoths (5 rows, pp. 210-212/PDF 211-213): the framework row (behemoths-overview, folding in the short 'Behemoth Powers' subsection -- a behemoth uses its attuned creature handler's base Traits, excluding Backgrounds and most Merits/Flaws but including Virtues), three named tiers as purchasable Artifact-Background options -- Fey Beast (Artifact • or ••, built around a guaranteed Knife-Hand Dream + Armament of Flesh natural attack), Daikaiju (Artifact •••, heavy natural armor plus 12 free mutation points), and Deep Wyld Horror (Artifact •••• or •••••, the heaviest-armored tier with natural weaponry equivalent to an attuned Magical Material artifact) -- and one unique, story-specific example, Ishiika (Artifact N/A), a legendary scorpion-behemoth once tamed by the lost Prince Balor. Ishiika is deliberately disposition gm-only rather than selectable: unlike the three generic tiers, it is a specific creature tied to one named NPC and explicitly too vast even for its own tamer to wield against Creation, illustrating the top of the power scale rather than offering a build a player follows -- this matches the task's instruction to skip pure Storyteller-facing creature stat blocks while still inventorying the genuinely player-facing Artifact-Background purchase options (the framework and the three generic tiers) that this section actually supplies. This also resolves a forward reference: the already-inventoried great-works-of-the-grace and unshaped-grace-transformation rows both name-check this material by page number without a cross-reference, since no behemoth rows existed yet.

The same eighth pass reviewed the short 'Nirupadhika, the Way' section (p. 211/PDF 212, immediately before Chapter Six begins) and resolved the open question flagged by prior passes about an apparent sixth Grace. DETERMINATION: Nirupadhika is neither a standard sixth playable Grace nor pure GM/setting lore -- the book explicitly introduces it as 'an example of one of the other shinma the raksha might tame' (associated with Awareness, Sail, and Survival), explicitly calls its Charms 'extremely rare,' and gives only two of them (versus 12 to 78 Charms for each of the five real Graces); it is never mentioned anywhere in the character-creation chapters (Three/Four) already inventoried, and no example raksha is shown starting play with a Way Grace. At the same time, its two Charms are fully rules-complete and genuinely usable in play: Forging the Way Grace (nirupadhika-the-way's framework row, plus forging-the-way-grace and perfect-reckoning-technique as selectable Charm rows) lets any raksha who already knows the existing Forging the Heart Grace Charm grant a Way Grace to a consenting creature as an artifact, exactly paralleling the four already-inventoried Forging the (Grace) Grace Charms (Cup/Ring/Staff/Sword) -- this is the first hint in the book that pattern could extend to any shinma a raksha tames, not just the five core Graces. Given this, Nirupadhika was inventoried as real, narrowly-scoped player-facing content (its own framework row plus its two Charms, all with full citations) rather than folded into the five-Grace model used elsewhere in this inventory or excluded outright as GM-only.

This same eighth pass also found and corrected a one-page offset in this file's own prior estimates for the Behemoths and Nirupadhika page ranges. Earlier passes (based on a pre-render skim) had estimated Behemoths at printed pp. 210-212/PDF 211-213 and Nirupadhika at printed p. 212/PDF 213. Direct visual confirmation against the rendered page images -- reading the printed folio number stamped on each page -- showed Behemoths' framework and 'Behemoth Powers' subsection begin on printed p. 210/PDF 211 as estimated, but that Deep Wyld Horror, Ishiika, and the entire Nirupadhika section (including both of its Charms) actually sit on printed p. 211/PDF 212, one page earlier than previously estimated; printed p. 212/PDF 213 is in fact a full-page illustration with no chapter text at all, marking the true end of Chapter Five ahead of Chapter Six: The Mountain Folk. All citations in this pass's new rows use the page numbers confirmed by direct visual reading, not the earlier estimate.

A ninth pass triaged the four chapters left unreviewed by every prior pass: Chapter One (Rakshastan, pp. 15-58/PDF 16-59), Chapter Two (The Raksha, pp. 59-90/PDF 60-91), Chapter Six (The Mountain Folk, pp. 213-294/PDF 214-295), and Chapter Seven (Storytelling, pp. 295-330/PDF 296-331), using the PDF's real text layer plus a full-text 'Merit'/'Flaw' search across all 331 pages of the book (not just these four chapters) as the primary goal. DEFINITIVE MERITS/FLAWS DETERMINATION: Exalted: The Fair Folk contains no dedicated Fair Folk-specific Merits/Flaws section anywhere in any of its seven chapters. The word 'Merit' appears exactly twice in the entire book, and 'Flaw' exactly twice (one of the four is shared, the passage on p. 210/PDF 211 already reviewed and inventoried as part of behemoths-overview): once in Chapter One (p. 18/PDF 19) referencing the unrelated, externally-defined 'Wyldwalk Merit' from the Exalted Players Guide by page number, not a Fair Folk Merit; once in Chapter Five (p. 168/PDF 169, already reviewed) referencing the externally-defined 'Enemy Flaw' from the Exalted Players Guide, again by page number; and once in Chapter Five's Behemoths section (p. 210/PDF 211, already reviewed and inventoried) noting in passing that a behemoth's borrowed Traits exclude 'Backgrounds and most Merits and Flaws.' None of these four incidental mentions constitutes or points to a Fair Folk-specific Merits/Flaws list, and no such list exists anywhere else in the book. This resolves the open question carried in every prior round of this inventory: like Lunar (see docs/references/exalted1e/lunar/README.md), Fair Folk has no dedicated Merits/Flaws subsection in its core sourcebook, confirmed by an exhaustive book-wide text search rather than chapter-by-chapter absence alone.

The same ninth pass's secondary goal -- scanning Chapters One, Two, Six and Seven for any other player-facing, character-creation-relevant mechanic (a new Charm, Background, artifact/item stat block, or named character-creation option) -- found exactly two, both now inventoried: Gossamer Manta (a purchasable Artifact Background level-three vehicle and Ring-shaping weapon, boxed in Chapter One's Rakshastan geography material on p. 38/PDF 39, functionally the same Wyld Artifacts category already inventoried from Chapter Five) and Fair Folk Experience and Training Time (Chapter Seven's post-creation experience-cost table and no-training-time-delay rule, boxed on p. 321/PDF 322, which fills a real gap since no prior pass had inventoried anything about post-creation advancement costs). Chapter Two (The Raksha) was confirmed to contain zero mechanical content of any kind -- no Charm, Background, Cost:, Essence, motes, dice-pool, or dot-rating language anywhere in its 32 pages -- and is pure worldbuilding/lore (raksha society, feeding customs, the courts' formation, connection to the land). Chapter One otherwise consists entirely of Storyteller-facing 'Hazard Rating' bestiary and environment stat blocks (Flame Gryphon, Lion Warrior, Sand Shark, Abacasteri, Gargoyle, Poppet, Homunculus, Stone Lion, Wood Wife, Doppelganger x2, Siaka-Man, the Glittering Desert, the Waters of Chaos, Unicorn, etc.) describing the dangers and wonders of Rakshastan's regions -- these were confirmed to be GM/encounter content, not player character options, and deliberately excluded from this inventory. Chapter Seven otherwise consists entirely of Storytelling advice (running a Fair Folk series, feeding as a theme, intrigue/courts-as-a-board framing, crossover-series notes with each other splat) with no further discrete player-facing mechanic found.

The same ninth pass confirmed Chapter Six: The Mountain Folk (pp. 213-294/PDF 214-295, 82 pages) is exactly what the task scoping anticipated: a separate, non-raksha playable-adjacent race (the Jadeborn) with its own extensive, wholly self-contained five-step character creation (its own Enlightened/Unenlightened split, its own three castes -- Artisan/Worker/Warrior -- its own Attribute/Ability priorities, its own modified-Backgrounds writeup, and its own experience-cost/training-time table on p. 232/PDF 233 directly paralleling the new fair-folk-experience-and-training-time row above), a full Charm section (pp. 244-276/PDF 245-277, roughly 190 Charm-stat-block hits), and a Mountain Folk-specific equipment/artifact catalog (pp. 276-284/PDF 277-285: Godstrike Oil, Synthetic Leather, several Resources-tier weapon tables, Essence-Scrying Visor, Skirmish Pike, Echo Jewel Platform, Talisman of Suspended Evocation, Dragon Sigh Wand, Myrmidon Carapace) followed by a Storyteller-facing 'Nameless Hordes' bestiary section (Darkbroods, hruggha, cephalid, Labyrinthines, Vodak, Underpeople) and Storytelling/anomaly advice (including the Chaos Seer antagonist type). None of this is Fair Folk (raksha) character-creation content, and per the task's explicit instruction, it is deliberately NOT inventoried in this file -- Chapter Six's Mountain Folk would be its own separate family/module decision, not part of Fair Folk (raksha) scope, if ever pursued. A close text search across the chapter for any raksha-specific interaction mechanic (rather than Mountain Folk's own lore) found only passive setting facts with no discrete player mechanic attached (e.g. p. 237/PDF 238 notes that 'any attempt by chaotic Fair Folk to feed on Mountain Folk souls automatically fails,' a one-line immunity fact about Jadeborn physiology, not a raksha Charm, Background, or selectable option), and nothing rose to the level of an inventoriable row.

With this ninth pass, Exalted: The Fair Folk has now been reviewed cover to cover -- every one of its seven chapters has been triaged or fully inventoried (263 rows total), Merits/Flaws are definitively confirmed absent book-wide, and the two remaining genuinely player-facing items outside the already-inventoried Chapters Three/Four/Five have been added. What remains out of scope by design: Chapter Three's Storyteller-only 'unshaped' Charm-suggestion sidebar (excluded per a prior pass), and Chapter Six's Mountain Folk character-creation/Charm/artifact system in its entirety (a separate race, noted above but never inventoried in this family's file).

73 of the 88 universal Players Guide Merits/Flaws apply to Fair Folk (37 merits + 36 flaws); 15 were excluded as either explicitly restricted to other splats by the source text's own header (Dragon-Blooded-only Legendary Breeding, Solar/Abyssal-only Taint's Warning, Solar/Lunar/Abyssal-only Eternal Vow, Lunars-only Limited Forms/Chimera, Celestial-Exalted-only Known Anathema/Permanent Caste Mark/Greater Curse/Throwback, Abyssals-and-Ghosts-only Death-Taint, Exalted-only Sworn Brotherhood/Beacon of Power) or ruled inapplicable by the raksha's own nature: Fair Folk are not Exalted at all, so Terrestrial Bloodline (requires a mortal Dragon-Blooded breeding lineage), Past Lives (requires an Exaltation-based Essence-reincarnation cycle raksha do not have) and Brigid's Heir (requires access to core Exalted Sorcery, which raksha replace entirely with their own Glamour Sorcery system) were all excluded as structural mismatches rather than by any explicit header restriction. Prodigy was included by analogy despite naming only Solar/Abyssal/Lunar as excluded (not Fair Folk), since a raksha's Caste/Favored Ability caps parallel Dragon-Blooded/Sidereal's (both left eligible in the source text) rather than the three excluded splats' reasoning -- flagged as a judgment call in that row's own notes. See the scope.notes field above for the full exclusion list and the adaptation judgment calls made for included rows (Large Size/Small reframed around Assumption-type shapeshifting Charms instead of Lunar forms; Cache/Debt reframed around the Gossamer Background instead of Resources, which raksha exclude entirely; Vice/Callous cross-referenced to Bedlam instead of the Great Curse; Unskilled reframed around Caste Abilities instead of Favored Abilities; and Destiny/Dark Fate/Unbidden Oracle included as selectable despite a flagged Loom-of-Fate conceptual tension, since raksha are canonically native to the Wyld outside Creation's Loom of Fate); each is also flagged verbatim in its own row's notes field.

An eleventh pass added two small sets of universal (non-splat-restricted) artifact catalog rows, bringing the total from 336 to 351. PART ONE (6 rows, no independent re-read): artifact-ghost-cestus, artifact-sling-bow-of-ice, artifact-the-golden-viper, artifact-land-ship, artifact-singing-staff, and artifact-eye-of-autochthon were copied verbatim (same id, name, mechanics, cost, and citation) from Lunar's already-verified transcription of the Exalted Storyteller's Companion's Chapter Four, 'Further Wonders' (printed pp. 77-80/PDF 78-81) -- a universal artifact catalog explicitly usable by 'normal humans,' not restricted to any splat. Because Fair Folk (raksha) are not Exalted, wear a physical 'Mote' as their body in Creation rather than having an Exalted anima, and use 'Glamour Sorcery' as their spell-casting framework, each row's compatibility and notes fields were individually rewritten (not just re-cited) to check the source's 'Essence-manipulating wielder'/'any Exalt' language against Fair Folk's own creation rules: fair-folk-creation-overview-common and -noble both confirm every raksha has an ordinary Essence rating (starting at 2) and mote pool (Essence x 10) exactly like the Creation-born Exalted, so all six items transfer without any genuine mechanical incompatibility. One item (artifact-eye-of-autochthon) was flagged with a non-blocking open question: its passive league-wide suppression of 'magical turbulence' plausibly overlaps with a raksha's own innate Wyld-immunity power (innate-powers-wyld-immunity) in ways the source text never anticipated for a non-Exalted, non-mortal bystander; this is left as an open interpretive question for a future Storyteller, not resolved in this pass, since neither source book gives guidance. PART TWO (9 rows freshly transcribed, no text layer, rendered via PyMuPDF at 2.2x zoom and read directly): a sixth source book, Savage Seas, was added to this family's manifest for its Chapter Four ('Creatures, Gods, Charms and Artifacts') 'Artifacts of the Waves' section, printed pp. 123-127/PDF 124-128 (the book's final mechanical content before the back cover on PDF 129) -- explicitly NOT including that same chapter's earlier 'Magics of the Sea' Charms section (printed pp. 114-122), which the book's own text restricts to Solar/Dragon-Blooded Exalted and remains correctly out of scope for Fair Folk. All 9 rows were transcribed and cited fresh: artifact-cargo-preservation-spindles (Artifact 1-3, p. 123), artifact-armor-of-aquatic-puissance (Artifact 4, p. 124), artifact-steelsilk-sails (Artifact 2, p. 124), artifact-storm-sapphire (Artifact 3-4, pp. 124-125), artifact-cord-of-winds (Artifact 1, pp. 125-126), artifact-wavecleaver-daiklaive (Artifact 2, p. 126), artifact-light-implosion-bow (Artifact 2-3, pp. 126-127), artifact-lightning-ballista (Artifact 3-4, p. 127), and artifact-ship-weapons-table (a reference-only summary of the two ship-weapon entries' stats, matching the precedent Abyssal's own derivation of this same Savage Seas material already set for this stat table). Two items surfaced during the required cover-to-cover read of pp. 123-128 that were not in the task brief's own 'already-confirmed' list: Cargo Preservation Spindles and Cord of Winds; both carry no splat restriction whatsoever in the source text (Cord of Winds is explicitly 'produced by even mortal sorcerers'). The Light Implosion Bow is the single strongest Fair-Folk fit found in this entire pass: its own text explicitly names 'any Exalted type and also Fair Folk and possibly others' as capable of channeling Essence into it -- the only artifact transcribed in either part of this pass to name raksha by name rather than requiring inference from an 'any Exalt' generalization. The Lightning Ballista carries the one explicitly flagged judgment call in Part Two: the source calls the weapon 'powerless in the hands of the unExalted,' but the actual mechanical requirement stated immediately beforehand is only that 'the firer must be able to manipulate Essence to activate them' -- interpreting the binding mechanical requirement rather than the more pointed illustrative word choice, a raksha (who manipulates Essence exactly as an Exalt does) qualifies, though a future reviewer could reasonably read 'unExalted' as a deliberate, splat-status-based exclusion instead; see that row's own notes. QUALITY NOTE: two low-zoom misreadings were caught and corrected via targeted high-zoom re-renders (clip regions around the two dense multi-column stat tables in this section) before this pass was considered complete -- the Storm Sapphire Effect Table's Black Sapphire column had several row-shifted values, and the Lightning Ballista's hearthstone-variant Artifact rating was initially misread as 3 dots instead of the correct 4 (matching the entry's own header, which groups 'hearthstone or elemental powered version' together at 4 dots). Both corrected rows carry a CORRECTION note documenting the fix. Every new row in both parts was individually checked against this family's own 'Mote' (capitalized, a raksha's physical body/shell) vs. 'motes' (lowercase, the Essence-pool currency) terminology distinction to avoid conflating the two; no genuine conflation was found, since the Storyteller's Companion and Savage Seas both use 'mote(s)' exclusively in the lowercase Essence-currency sense.
